summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is lawful in Madagascar only from age 21. Article 331 of the Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment. The age of consent is unequal, so a trans visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 carries a criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not. In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint; the mother was allegedly acting to cover an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders offered the younger woman conversion therapy during the proceedings.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex, whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names gender identity as a cause of absolute nullity of marriage, which is a direct legal exposure for a trans person whose marriage is examined under that provision. No civil union or other form of partner recognition exists.

Adoption is restricted. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses, so a trans visitor resident in the country with a partner has no route to joint adoption.

Data protection law treats sexual life and orientation as sensitive. Article 18 of Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Article 2 of Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus protects sexual orientation as sensitive data. The provisions matter where a visitor's medical or financial records would otherwise record a partner or a transition history.

Health policy addresses trans and same-sex health needs mainly through HIV programming. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions protecting vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission.

The government rejected trans and LGBT protections at its fourth Universal Periodic Review in January 2025, which carried 235 recommendations. It declined recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, responded that refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.

Public expression is constrained by administrative action. In early July 2021 the government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of incitement to debauchery.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised as such, but it is widely considered socially unacceptable and many people conceal it to keep their jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused the couple of promising homosexuality.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar has no general sodomy offence; the criminal exposure in the Penal Code is confined to the unequal age threshold in Article 331, which distinguishes it from jurisdictions in the region that criminalise same-sex conduct outright. A BBC News Pidgin survey in July 2020 placed Madagascar among the roughly 22 of 53 African states that had decriminalised same-sex activity, while noting that the under-21 offence remained.

The one documented prosecution, in 2020, began with a complaint by a family member rather than with police action, and no source records a standing enforcement campaign against adult same-sex conduct. Visitors should read the risk as arising from a complaint-driven process, in which a relative, landlord or employer can set the machinery in motion, rather than from routine policing.
localsOnly:
Malagasy LGBT people describe concealment as a condition of employment and social peace, maintaining separate networks and coded language rather than open community life. Residents cannot marry a partner of the same sex or jointly adopt, and the nullity provision naming gender identity means a trans resident's existing marriage can be challenged on that ground.

Advocacy is organised but small and publicly contested. The six organisations that signed the response to the January 2025 Universal Periodic Review work on legal equality and against impunity for anti-LGBT violence, in a setting where the government has refused to commit to either. Transgender sex workers, documented in the 2011 State Department report as targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and murder, remain the most exposed group in the sources.

Health access runs through the HIV framework: Act No. 2005-040 requires programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups and names men who have sex with men, sex workers, young people and mobile populations as groups entitled to specific protection. Conversion therapy is not a state programme in the sources, but religious leaders offered it to the young woman at the centre of the 2020 case.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records the number of prosecutions brought under Article 331, so the frequency of enforcement against the under-21 offence is unresolved. Whether the data protection provisions in Law No. 2014-038 and Law No. 2017-045 are enforced in practice, and whether they cover records held by private clinics or employers, is not sourced.

No source addresses police or border-screening practice towards trans travellers, document and marker rules at ports of entry, or access to bathrooms and single-sex facilities. No trans-specific hate-crime or anti-discrimination statute was located in the inventory, and the position on legal gender recognition is not documented here. The most detailed account of violence against transgender sex workers dates from the 2011 State Department report and no figure with a denominator accompanies it.
